chunks.title: for statement
chunks.text: The for statement creates a loop with three optional expressions: initialization, condition and afterthought. for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) runs the body n times. Use break to exit and continue to skip an iteration.
chunks.nudge: Think about your loop's three parts: where does it start, when does it stop, and how does it move forward?

chunks.title: for...of statement
chunks.text: for...of iterates over iterable objects (arrays, strings, maps, sets). for (const item of array) gives each element in order. Use it when you need values, not indices.
chunks.nudge: If you need each value one by one, for...of is the simplest way to walk through an array.

chunks.title: while statement
chunks.text: The while statement executes its body as long as the condition is true. Something inside the loop must change the condition, or it runs forever.
chunks.nudge: Ask what changes each time through the loop so the condition eventually becomes false.

chunks.title: if...else statement
chunks.text: if (condition) executes a block when the condition is truthy. Add else if for more branches and else for a fallback. Only one branch runs. JavaScript uses truthy/falsy: 0, '', null, undefined and NaN are falsy.
chunks.nudge: Check which branch runs first; the first truthy condition wins. Watch out for falsy surprises like 0 or empty string.

chunks.title: Comparison operators
chunks.text: JavaScript has == (loose equality, with type coercion), === (strict equality, no coercion), <, >, <=, >=, != and !==. Prefer === and !== to avoid coercion surprises. Comparisons return a boolean.
chunks.nudge: Make sure you're using === instead of ==, and check your boundary: does the edge case need >= or >?

chunks.title: Arithmetic operators
chunks.text: Numbers support +, -, *, / (always floating-point), % (remainder) and ** (exponentiation). There is no integer division operator; use Math.floor(a / b) for floor division. Be aware that 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 due to floating-point precision.
chunks.nudge: Double-check which operation the task asks for; dividing in JavaScript always gives a float unless you explicitly floor it.

chunks.title: Math object
chunks.text: Math provides static methods: Math.floor(), Math.ceil(), Math.round(), Math.abs(), Math.max(), Math.min(), Math.pow(base, exp), Math.sqrt(), Math.random(). Math.floor(x) rounds toward negative infinity.
chunks.nudge: If you need a specific math operation, check the Math object — it likely has what you need.

chunks.title: Function declaration and arrow functions
chunks.text: Functions are declared with function name(params) {} or as arrow functions: const fn = (params) => expression (implicit return) or (params) => { statements } (explicit return needed). A function without return gives undefined.
chunks.nudge: Make sure your function returns a value; arrow functions with {} need an explicit return statement.

chunks.title: return statement
chunks.text: return exits the function and optionally gives a value to the caller. A function that reaches the end without return gives undefined. return on its own (no value) gives undefined too.
chunks.nudge: Check that every code path through your function reaches a return with the right value.

chunks.title: Type conversions
chunks.text: Number(str) converts a string to a number (NaN if it fails). parseInt(str, 10) parses an integer; always pass the radix. String(val) converts to string. typeof checks the type. The + operator with a string triggers concatenation, not addition.
chunks.nudge: If your code concatenates instead of adding, check whether one operand is a string that needs Number() first.

chunks.title: Template literals
chunks.text: Template literals use backticks: `Hello, ${name}!`. Expressions inside ${} are evaluated and converted to strings. They can span multiple lines. Tagged templates allow custom processing.
chunks.nudge: Use backticks and ${} to embed values in a string instead of concatenation.

chunks.title: String methods
chunks.text: Strings are immutable. Common methods: .length (property), .includes(), .indexOf(), .slice(start, end), .substring(), .split(), .trim(), .toUpperCase(), .toLowerCase(), .replace(), .replaceAll(), .startsWith(), .endsWith(). Methods return new strings.
chunks.nudge: Remember strings are immutable — .replace() returns a new string; assign it back.

chunks.title: Arrays
chunks.text: Arrays are ordered lists: const arr = [1, 2, 3]. Access by index (0-based). Mutating: .push(), .pop(), .shift(), .unshift(), .splice(). Non-mutating: .slice(), .concat(), .includes(), .indexOf(), .join(). .length gives the count.
chunks.nudge: Check whether you need to change the array in place (push/splice) or get a new one (slice/concat).

chunks.title: Array iteration methods
chunks.text: .map(fn) transforms each element and returns a new array. .filter(fn) keeps elements where fn returns true. .reduce(fn, init) accumulates a value. .forEach(fn) runs fn on each element (no return value). .find(fn) returns the first match or undefined. .every(fn) and .some(fn) test conditions.
chunks.nudge: If you want to transform every element, use .map(); if you want to keep only some, use .filter(); if you want a single accumulated value, use .reduce().

chunks.title: Objects
chunks.text: Objects are key-value collections: { key: value }. Access with obj.key or obj['key']. Object.keys(), Object.values(), Object.entries() return arrays. Use the in operator to check if a key exists. Destructuring: const { a, b } = obj.
chunks.nudge: If you need to check whether a key exists, use 'key' in obj or obj.hasOwnProperty('key').

chunks.title: Map and Set
chunks.text: Map stores key-value pairs with any key type: new Map(), .set(k, v), .get(k), .has(k), .delete(k), .size. Set stores unique values: new Set(), .add(v), .has(v), .delete(v), .size. Both are iterable with for...of.
chunks.nudge: If you need unique values or fast lookups by key, consider Set or Map instead of arrays and objects.

chunks.title: Spread and rest syntax
chunks.text: Spread (...) expands an iterable into individual elements: [...arr1, ...arr2] merges arrays; { ...obj1, ...obj2 } merges objects. Rest (...args) collects remaining arguments into an array.
chunks.nudge: Use spread to combine or copy arrays/objects without mutating the originals.

chunks.title: try...catch
chunks.text: try { ... } catch (e) { ... } catches runtime errors. e.message describes the error. Add finally for cleanup that always runs. throw new Error('message') raises an error.
chunks.nudge: If your code might fail on certain inputs, wrap the risky part in try/catch and handle the error.

chunks.title: null and undefined
chunks.text: undefined means a variable was declared but not assigned, or a function returned nothing. null is an intentional 'no value'. Use === null or === undefined for checks. The ?? (nullish coalescing) operator provides a default for null/undefined only.
chunks.nudge: If your function returns undefined when you expect a value, check that every path has a return statement.

chunks.title: Array.prototype.sort()
chunks.text: .sort() sorts in place and by default converts elements to strings, so [10, 2, 1].sort() gives [1, 10, 2]. For numbers use .sort((a, b) => a - b). Return negative if a < b, positive if a > b, 0 if equal.
chunks.nudge: If sorting numbers gives unexpected results, you need a compare function: .sort((a, b) => a - b).

chunks.title: Conditional (ternary) operator
chunks.text: condition ? exprIfTrue : exprIfFalse evaluates one of two expressions. Useful for short inline decisions. Avoid nesting ternaries deeply — use if/else for readability.
chunks.nudge: A ternary is a compact if/else for expressions. Make sure both branches return the right type.
